title: The Korean War, 1950–1953
summary: How a divided Korea went to war, how the United Nations and then China were drawn in, why the front ended close to where it began, and what the war cost. Twelve scenes, with maps that follow War Focus through the war's turning points.

scenes.title: The Korean War
scenes.narration: Before dawn on 25 June 1950 the army of North Korea crossed the 38th parallel and invaded South Korea. Within months the war had drawn in the United States and fifteen other countries under the flag of the United Nations, and then the People's Republic of China. It ended in July 1953 with an armistice, not a peace, close to where it began, and Korea is divided still.

scenes.title: A divided country, 1945–1950
scenes.narration: Korea had been a Japanese colony since 1910. When Japan surrendered in August 1945, the United States proposed and the Soviet Union accepted a temporary line along the 38th parallel, with Soviet troops occupying the north and American troops the south. Talks on a single government failed, and in 1948 two rival states were proclaimed: the Republic of Korea under Syngman Rhee in Seoul, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea under Kim Il-sung in Pyongyang. Each claimed the whole peninsula, and by 1949 their armies were clashing along the border while the South crushed a Communist-led insurgency.

scenes.title: Stalin's consent, 1949–1950
scenes.narration: Kim Il-sung pressed Joseph Stalin for permission to reunify Korea by force, and in 1949 Stalin refused. Soviet records opened in the 1990s show that he changed his mind early in 1950, after the Communist victory in China and the first Soviet atomic test, and approved the plan in Moscow in April, on condition that Mao Zedong agreed. Mao gave his consent in May, and Soviet military advisers helped to plan the attack.

scenes.title: The invasion, June to September 1950
scenes.narration: North Korea attacked with tanks and heavy artillery that the South lacked, and took Seoul three days later. The United States rushed troops from occupied Japan, but by early August they and the South Korean army had been pushed back to a perimeter around the port of Pusan, in the south-east corner of the peninsula. As the front moved, both sides killed civilians they suspected of siding with the enemy: South Korean forces executed tens of thousands of political prisoners and suspected leftists, and the North's occupiers killed officials, police and others they judged hostile.

scenes.title: The United Nations responds
scenes.narration: The Security Council met on the day of the invasion and demanded a North Korean withdrawal, and on 27 June it called on members to help the South. The Soviet Union could have vetoed both resolutions, but it was boycotting the Council because China's seat was still held by the Nationalist government on Taiwan. President Harry Truman committed American air, naval and then ground forces, and in July the Council placed the troops sent by member states under a unified command led by the United States, with General Douglas MacArthur in command.

visual.text: Recommends that the Members of the United Nations furnish such assistance to the Republic of Korea as may be necessary to repel the armed attack and to restore international peace and security in the area.

scenes.title: Inchon and the march north, September–October 1950
scenes.narration: On 15 September MacArthur landed two divisions at Inchon, far behind the North Korean lines, and as the defenders of Pusan broke out, Seoul was retaken by the end of the month. South Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel on 1 October, and after a General Assembly resolution on 7 October backed the unification of Korea, American and other forces followed. Pyongyang fell on 19 October, and a week later South Korean units reached the Yalu River on the Chinese border.

scenes.title: China enters the war, October 1950 – January 1951
scenes.narration: China's premier, Zhou Enlai, had warned through India's ambassador that China would intervene if American troops crossed the parallel, and Washington discounted the warning. Chinese People's Volunteers under Peng Dehuai began crossing the Yalu on 19 October, struck in late October and, at the end of November, launched a general offensive that sent the United Nations forces into a long retreat. Pyongyang was abandoned in early December, American marines fought their way out from the Chosin Reservoir, and on 4 January 1951 Seoul fell for the second time.

scenes.title: Ridgway, MacArthur and a limited war, 1951
scenes.narration: Meeting Truman on Wake Island in October 1950, MacArthur had assured him that China was unlikely to intervene in strength. After the Chinese offensives, General Matthew Ridgway took command of the Eighth Army and rallied it, and by the end of March 1951 Seoul had been retaken and the front pushed back to around the 38th parallel. MacArthur argued in public for carrying the war into China, and on 11 April Truman dismissed him, choosing to keep the war limited to Korea.

scenes.title: Talks and stalemate, 1951–1953
scenes.narration: From July 1951 the two sides negotiated, first at Kaesong and then at Panmunjom, while fighting went on for hills along a line that barely moved. The longest dispute was over prisoners: many Chinese and North Korean prisoners did not want to go home, and the United Nations Command refused to return them by force. American bombing devastated North Korea's towns, dams and power stations, and the war dragged on until both sides, and Stalin's successors after his death in March 1953, were ready to settle.

scenes.title: The armistice, 27 July 1953
scenes.narration: The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 by the commanders of the United Nations Command, the Korean People's Army and the Chinese People's Volunteers; South Korea's president, Syngman Rhee, refused to sign. It created a demilitarised zone four kilometres wide along the final front line and arranged the exchange of prisoners, with neutral nations supervising those who refused to go home. The peace conference held at Geneva in 1954 failed, and no peace treaty has ever been signed.

visual.text: … an armistice which will ensure a complete cessation of hostilities and of all acts of armed force in Korea until a final peaceful settlement is achieved.

scenes.title: The human cost
scenes.narration: No one knows exactly how many people died in the Korean War, so this chart shows ranges. The Peace Research Institute Oslo estimates that between about 645,000 and 1.5 million soldiers and civilians were killed in the fighting itself, more than half of them in the first year. Civilians killed in massacres, or by hunger and disease, are not in that count, and estimates of all Korean deaths, soldiers and civilians together, are well above a million.

visual.title: Battle deaths in the Korean War, year by year: PRIO's range of estimates
visual.note: Deaths in combat among all the armies, including civilians killed in the fighting. One-sided killings of civilians and deaths from hunger and disease are not counted. PRIO's best estimate for the whole war is about 995,000.

scenes.title: Two Koreas
scenes.narration: The war fixed the division of Korea, with American troops stationed in the South under a defence treaty and North Korea allied to China. It also hardened the Cold War far beyond Korea: the United States rearmed on a large scale, and NATO became a standing military alliance with a permanent command. South Korea, ruled for most of the next three decades by authoritarian governments, became a democracy in 1987 and one of the world's leading industrial economies, while North Korea is still ruled by Kim Il-sung's family and has built nuclear weapons.
